𝗪𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬, 𝟏𝟗𝟗𝟖.⁣
⁣
Let’s get this out of the way first: Wild Things (1998) is pure guilty pleasure. Filthy, sweaty, unapologetic pleasure. This movie might just be the greatest guilty pleasure movie of the 90s. On the surface it looks like some sleazy late-night cable flick with teenagers, bikinis, and a swamp. And yet, once you dive in, you realize it’s also one of the cleverest, most shamelessly entertaining noirs of its time.⁣
⁣
The cast is perfect in all the wrong ways. Matt Dillon has never been slimier, walking a line between guidance counselor and con artist with a grin you instantly don’t trust. Denise Richards gives the performance of her career (and the pool scene is now basically pop culture legend). Neve Campbell plays against type as a dangerous, damaged outcast and completely sells it. Kevin Bacon does his usual stoic detective thing, but then surprises you with… well, let’s just say the infamous “shower reveal.” And then there’s Bill Murray, parachuting in to steal every scene with his perfectly greasy comic timing. ⁣
⁣
The best thing about Wild Things (1998) is that it knows exactly what it is: guilty pleasure cinema. It doesn’t care about subtlety, it doesn’t care about realism, and it certainly doesn’t care about good taste. Instead, it amplifies every cliché, and somehow spins it into something unforgettable. From the glossy Florida settings to George S. Clinton’s moody score, it has the vibe of a late-90s music video that accidentally turned into a noir classic.⁣
⁣
What are your thoughts on 𝗪𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 (𝟏𝟗𝟗𝟖)? 💭

source_details.synopsis: Wild Things is a 1998 American erotic thriller film directed by John McNaughton and starring Matt Dillon, Kevin Bacon, Neve Campbell, Denise Richards, Theresa Russell, Robert Wagner, and Bill Murray. It follows a high school guidance counselor in South Florida who is accused of rape by two female students and a series of subsequent revelations after a police officer begins investigating the alleged crimes. Wild Things was released by Sony Pictures Releasing on March 20, 1998 and received mixed to positive reviews from critics while grossing $67.2 million against a $20 million budget.
